claim_verdicts.slide: Recall as a Silently-Violated SLO
claim_verdicts.bullet: ANN search achieves speed by accepting silent recall losses — vectors disappear from results without any error notification
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search achieves speed gains by accepting 'silent' recall losses — vectors disappearing from results without explicit notification to users.

claim_verdicts.slide: Recall as a Silently-Violated SLO
claim_verdicts.bullet: Even with a substantial latency budget, recall@1 may reach only 0.9, meaning the true nearest neighbour is absent in ~10% of queries
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: At k=240 (35ms latency), recall@1 reaches only 0.9, meaning 'for about 10% of the queries, the true top nearest neighbor is missing from the result.'

claim_verdicts.slide: Recall as a Silently-Violated SLO
claim_verdicts.bullet: Recall degrades silently as the dataset grows: a 10%+ drop from 50k to 200k vectors with fixed index parameters has been observed
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Retrieval quality degrades silently as the vector database grows, even when latency remains stable. Recall drops by 10%+ as database grows from 50k to 200k.

claim_verdicts.slide: Metadata Filtering and ANN — The Interaction Problem
claim_verdicts.bullet: Post-filtering (run ANN first, then apply predicate) can return zero results when a selective filter eliminates all ANN candidates
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: In post-filtering scenarios, none of the nearest documents may match the filter, resulting in 0% recall regardless of vector index performance.

claim_verdicts.slide: Metadata Filtering and ANN — The Interaction Problem
claim_verdicts.bullet: Pre-filtering (apply predicate first, then run ANN on the subset) degrades to brute force when the filtered subset is large
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Pre-filtering ('filter-then-search') guarantees correctness, but if that subset is large you end up doing a near-linear scan.

claim_verdicts.slide: Metadata Filtering and ANN — The Interaction Problem
claim_verdicts.bullet: Tight filters cause tail latencies of 200–300 ms in post-filter fallback engines
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: engines relying on post-filter fallbacks can spike to 200–300 ms under filtering in tail latencies.

claim_verdicts.slide: Metadata Filtering and ANN — The Interaction Problem
claim_verdicts.bullet: Dedicated vector databases such as Qdrant and Weaviate address this by integrating filters inside HNSW graph traversal; pgvector performs post-filter on a candidate set, making selective queries scan hundreds of thousands of candidates
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Qdrant indexes payload fields and runs filters inside the HNSW graph traversal, outperforming pgvector's post-filter approach for selective queries. pgvector: post-filter on candidate set; selective queries (10% selectivity on 5M vectors) scan 500K candidates.
claim_verdicts.issue: The source excerpt explicitly confirms that Qdrant integrates filters inside HNSW traversal, but does not mention Weaviate by name. The bullet asserts 'Qdrant and Weaviate' both address this via in-graph filtering, but only Qdrant is confirmed by the cited source. Weaviate is an unsupported addition.
claim_verdicts.suggested_fix: Dedicated vector databases such as Qdrant address this by integrating filters inside HNSW graph traversal; pgvector performs post-filter on a candidate set, making selective queries scan hundreds of thousands of candidates.

claim_verdicts.slide: Choosing a Vector Store — pgvector vs. Dedicated Databases
claim_verdicts.bullet: pgvector is the appropriate default for datasets under ~2M vectors when Postgres is already in the stack, offering full SQL join capability and zero additional infrastructure
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: pgvector is the default choice for RAG systems under 2M vectors... Use pgvector if you're already running Postgres, you want vectors alongside your application data, and your dataset is under 10M vectors — no separate service, no sync layer, and no new infrastructure.

claim_verdicts.slide: Choosing a Vector Store — pgvector vs. Dedicated Databases
claim_verdicts.bullet: Above 5–10M vectors or for sub-20ms p95 latency requirements, dedicated vector databases become preferable
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: For 5M+ vectors and sub-20ms p95 latency, Pinecone delivers with no configuration but at 3-8x cost vs Supabase Postgres. Above 5-10 million vectors, pgvector requires careful tuning of shared_buffers, work_mem, and HNSW parameters to maintain fast queries.

claim_verdicts.slide: Choosing a Vector Store — pgvector vs. Dedicated Databases
claim_verdicts.bullet: Qdrant provides best-in-class filtered search by integrating predicates inside HNSW traversal; Pinecone offers zero-ops managed scale at a 3–8x cost premium; Milvus is designed for billion-vector sharded deployments
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Qdrant indexes payload fields and runs filters inside the HNSW graph traversal, outperforming pgvector's post-filter approach for selective queries. For 5M+ vectors and sub-20ms p95 latency, Pinecone delivers with no configuration but at 3-8x cost vs Supabase Postgres. Use Milvus if you're working at billion-vector scale: it's built for massive datasets and has the most mature sharding and partitioning.

claim_verdicts.slide: Choosing a Vector Store — pgvector vs. Dedicated Databases
claim_verdicts.bullet: Past 2M vectors on a single Postgres instance, index build times can exceed 20 minutes
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Past 2M vectors on a single Postgres instance, you'll see index build times exceed 20 minutes.

claim_verdicts.slide: RAG Is Not a Single Similarity Lookup
claim_verdicts.bullet: RAG retrieval is a two-stage data pipeline: stage 1 (retrieval) maximizes recall by casting a wide net; stage 2 (reranking) maximizes precision by scoring the retrieved set more carefully
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Stage 1: Retrieval (Recall)...cast a wide net. Stage 2: Reranking (Precision)...sort the pile...use a Cross-Encoder to read the top 50 candidates and push the best ones to the top.

claim_verdicts.slide: RAG Is Not a Single Similarity Lookup
claim_verdicts.bullet: Chunking is the schema-design decision that precedes both stages: chunk size, boundary policy, and structure determine which information units are indexed and retrieved
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: The paper's central finding is that no single granularity is optimal across queries — the optimal chunk size is query-dependent. This directly supports framing chunking strategy as a design decision with performance consequences analogous to schema design in databases.

claim_verdicts.slide: RAG Is Not a Single Similarity Lookup
claim_verdicts.bullet: There is no universal optimal chunk size — smaller chunks (64–128 tokens) favor fact-based queries while larger chunks (512–1024 tokens) favor contextual queries
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Smaller chunks (64-128 tokens) are optimal for datasets with concise, fact-based answers, whereas larger chunks (512-1024 tokens) improve retrieval in datasets requiring broader contextual understanding.

claim_verdicts.slide: Chunking Strategy — A Schema Design Decision
claim_verdicts.bullet: Large chunks can exceed token limits or include irrelevant content, reducing precision; small chunks may lack surrounding context needed for accurate generation
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Large chunks can exceed token limits or retrieve irrelevant information, reducing retrieval precision, while small chunks might miss the context necessary for effective generation.

claim_verdicts.slide: Chunking Strategy — A Schema Design Decision
claim_verdicts.bullet: Chunk size is a design tradeoff: increasing it improves context availability but dilutes specificity; decreasing it sharpens specificity but loses context
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: As chunk size grows, a fixed-size vector must compress increasingly diverse information, inevitably losing fine-grained details. Conversely, smaller chunks preserve specificity but sacrifice the surrounding context needed to understand meaning.

claim_verdicts.slide: Chunking Strategy — A Schema Design Decision
claim_verdicts.bullet: This tradeoff is directly analogous to schema-design decisions about table granularity — the right answer depends on the dominant query pattern
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: the best-performing chunk size varies substantially across queries, even when querying the same corpus. Standard practice treats chunk size as a one-time tuning parameter: choose a value, measure average performance, iterate until satisfied, then deploy.
claim_verdicts.issue: The source file for claim:agde:045 (AI21 Labs blog on query-dependent chunking) contains no mention of schema-design decisions, table granularity, or any database design analogy. The bullet asserts a specific analogy — chunk size tradeoff is 'directly analogous to schema-design decisions about table granularity' — that is entirely absent from the cited source. The source supports only the query-dependency of chunk size and the precision-context tradeoff, not the database schema framing.
claim_verdicts.suggested_fix: Chunk size is a query-dependent design tradeoff — the best-performing size varies substantially across queries, making it a decision that should be driven by the dominant query pattern rather than treated as a fixed one-time tuning parameter.

claim_verdicts.slide: Hybrid Retrieval — BM25 + Dense ANN
claim_verdicts.bullet: BM25 sparse retrieval and dense ANN retrieval fail in complementary directions: BM25 excels at exact-match queries (product codes, error codes, rare identifiers) but has no semantic understanding
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: You can't pick between BM25 and dense retrieval. You need both. They fail in opposite ways. Exact identifiers survive [in BM25]. Error codes, ticket IDs, API endpoints, function names, configuration keys — anything that needs to be precisely correct rather than semantically similar. BM25 isn't about semantic understanding.

claim_verdicts.slide: Hybrid Retrieval — BM25 + Dense ANN
claim_verdicts.bullet: Dense retrieval handles paraphrase and conceptual queries but may assign low scores to exact rare-term matches — making hybrid retrieval the recommended baseline for production RAG
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: [Dense retrieval] treats symbols as noise. Embedding models treat tokens like 'E4392' or '/api/v2/users' as less important than readable text. Production retrieval needs both the lexical precision of BM25 and the semantic recall of vector search. Hybrid search recovers both signals and produces far more useful candidate sets for RAG.

claim_verdicts.slide: Hybrid Retrieval — BM25 + Dense ANN
claim_verdicts.bullet: RRF (Reciprocal Rank Fusion), introduced at SIGIR 2009, is the standard fusion algorithm: it computes RRF(c) = Σ 1/(rank_i(c) + k) with k=60, operating on rank positions rather than raw scores
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Venue: Proceedings of the 32nd international ACM SIGIR conference on Research and development in information retrieval (SIGIR 2009). RRF formula: RRF(c) = Σ 1/(rank_i(c) + k), where rank_i(c) is the rank of document c in retrieval system i, and k=60 is the standard smoothing constant. RRF relies solely on the ranking positions of the combined mechanisms, which makes it independent of their specific implementations.

claim_verdicts.slide: Code — Reciprocal Rank Fusion
claim_verdicts.bullet: RRF operates on rank positions, not raw scores — this avoids the score-incompatibility problem between BM25 and cosine similarity
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: RRF relies solely on the ranking positions of the combined mechanisms, which makes it independent of their specific implementations. Instead of trying to somehow normalize arbitrary scores, RRF ignores the scores entirely and focuses on rank.

claim_verdicts.slide: How Hybrid Retrieval Improves Recall
claim_verdicts.bullet: Measured Recall@5: dense-only 0.587, BM25-only 0.644, hybrid RRF 0.695, hybrid RRF + neural reranker 0.816
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: A two-stage pipeline combining hybrid retrieval with neural reranking achieves Recall@5 of 0.816 compared to 0.695 for Hybrid RRF alone (+17.4%), 0.644 for BM25 (+26.7%), and 0.587 for dense retrieval (+39.0%).

claim_verdicts.slide: How Hybrid Retrieval Improves Recall
claim_verdicts.bullet: The hybrid recall gain is attributable to BM25 pulling in relevant documents the dense retriever ranked too low — not to reranking, which cannot improve recall
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: re-ranking does not help recall because it works within the already-retrieved set. The hybrid improvement on recall was the BM25 component pulling in the additional relevant documents.
